# Node.js Gotchas

> Known Node.js runtime patterns that cause silent failures or hard-to-debug errors.

## Entries

- [Global fetch() with no User-Agent is rejected (HTTP 400) by some external APIs](fetch-user-agent.md): Node/undici's default User-Agent gets 400'd by Scryfall (and likely other APIs); the swallowed error silently falls back to a data source missing fields. Always set an explicit User-Agent. HIGH.
- [Scripts walking `git ls-files` crash on tracked-but-missing files](git-ls-files-missing-on-disk.md): git ls-files lists the index, not the disk; an AD-status file (staged then deleted) crashes naive readFileSync loops in guard scripts right when the tree is messy. Guard ENOENT and skip. MEDIUM.
- [BullMQ delayed jobs are silently lost when Redis is redeployed](bullmq-redis-delayed-jobs-lost.md): A Redis redeploy/upgrade flushes the BullMQ keyspace even on a same-volume tag bump; repeatable jobs self-heal on boot but one-off DELAYED jobs vanish, leaving DB rows PENDING forever with no error to catch. Add an absence-detecting watchdog and scan for orphans after any Redis swap. HIGH.
- [AbortSignal.timeout() on fetch() covers body streaming, not just the response](abortsignal-timeout-covers-body-streaming.md): The signal bounds the whole fetch, so a header-sized timeout aborts a large download mid-stream; fetch() resolves fine and the TimeoutError surfaces later inside the parser, where a consumer that treats stream errors as end-of-input yields a silently partial dataset. Leave streaming reads unbounded, or use an idle timeout. HIGH.
- [A leaked timer calling process.exit() disguises a test-suite hang as a fast failure](leaked-exit-timer-masks-test-hang.md): a shutdown watchdog timer left uncleared by a mock that never invokes its callback fires after the suite finishes, so "N passed" is followed by exit 1 from application code -- and it masks a separate open-handle hang, so fixing the timer makes CI hang instead of fail. Timing-dependent, hence "passes locally, fails in CI". Fix with fake timers, not by unref'ing the production timer. HIGH.
- [A job's one-shot kickoff timer outlives graceful shutdown unless it joins the interval's registry](unregistered-kickoff-timer-survives-shutdown.md): the "run soon, then on a schedule" pattern arms a setTimeout kickoff beside its setInterval, and registering only the interval leaves a live handle shutdown cannot cancel -- it fires after Redis and the DB pool are closed, and under Jest it hangs the worker (force-exit + 0 locally, a runner that never exits in CI) while every test reports green. Push the kickoff too; unref alone hides the hang and leaves the shutdown race. Includes the per-file --detectOpenHandles bisect. HIGH.
- [execSync lets the shell eat a glob meant for the child program](execsync-shell-expands-child-glob.md): `execSync` runs via `/bin/sh -c`, so an unquoted glob is expanded by the shell before the child (git/find/rsync/grep) can interpret it -- and a git pathspec's `*` crosses `/` while a shell's does not, so `src/*.ts` silently collapses from 1920 files to 1. Damage is per-argument and depends on whether the shell found a match, so some patterns stay accidentally correct and mask the rest (one CI guard scanned 35% of its files and reported clean). Use `execFileSync` with an argv array, and assert a file-count floor. HIGH.
- [Switching a directory scan to node:fs/promises does not unblock the event loop when JSON.parse is half the cost](async-fs-does-not-unblock-parse-bound-scan.md): the reflexive "no sync fs on a request path" fix converts only the I/O; JSON.parse has no async form, so a 305 ms blocking scan of 370 files/128 MB drops to ~152 ms and keeps stalling every other request. Both obvious metrics improve (own latency, lint passes), so the half-fix ships -- the symptom to measure is CROSS-request latency (a trivial /health went 117 ms -> 1246 ms under 4 concurrent calls). Cache the projection instead: 1.4 ms warm, 11 MB retained. HIGH.
- [A parent-directory mtime cache key never observes an edit to a file inside it](parent-dir-mtime-misses-file-edits.md): a directory's mtime moves when an entry is added/removed/renamed, never when an existing file's contents change -- so a one-stat `stat(ROOT)` key rebuilds correctly on create and delete (the cases you test first) and serves edits stale forever. Atomic rename writes bump the FILE's own directory, not ROOT. Key on each file's mtime (1.5 ms for 370 stats) and mutation-test the check, or the suite proves nothing. HIGH.
- [A fallback that routes back through the failing dependency turns a blip into an outage](fallback-through-failing-dependency.md): the "fast path + graceful fallback" shape hides two compounding defects -- the per-item fallback calls the SAME service the batch just failed against (an amplifier, not a mitigation), and an empty result container conflates "the request failed" with "the query matched nothing", so choosing the recovery from `map.size === 0` picks the dangerous branch. A pg pool capped at max:10 against one import's own 13-way fan-out threw, became an HTTP 500, was read as "no rows", and stranded 19 of 22 records PERSISTED WITH NO DATA -- which downstream joins silently drop, so it reads as "imports are slow" rather than corruption. Retry the fast path (never on 4xx), return the transport outcome (`degraded`) beside the map, fan out only on a true outage (a genuine no-match reaches an external rate-limited API where the pacing is load-bearing), and surface the degradation to the caller. HIGH.
- [A per-key mutex held by middleware deadlocks any handler that re-acquires it, and poisons that key forever](middleware-mutex-reacquired-in-handler.md): the "serialize writes per resource" middleware wraps the whole chain in `withLock(key, () => next())`, so a handler that reaches for the same helper for its own read-modify-write acquires it twice and waits on a turn that cannot release until it returns. Only the cross-process file lock is bounded (ELOCKED -> 503); the in-memory FIFO stage is a bare `await prev`, so it hangs forever AND never yields its queue slot -- one bad request takes that key out of service until the process restarts. Reads skip the lock and stay fast, so it reads as data corruption, and the lock sits upstream of routing and auth, so a nonexistent route and an unauthenticated request hang too (which is also how you localize it in three requests). Route tests that mount the handler on a bare app without the middleware pass while prod deadlocks. HIGH.
- [JSON.stringify and Go's encoding/json disagree, so a body signed in Node verifies nowhere](json-canonicalization-diverges-from-go.md): a signature covers bytes, and the two standard libraries escape strings differently -- Go escapes `<` `>` `&` by default (fixable with SetEscapeHTML(false)) and escapes U+2028/U+2029 **unconditionally**, with no flag, while JSON.stringify escapes neither; one free-text field (contentType, description, filename) carrying an invisible U+2028 signs cleanly on the server and fails verification on every endpoint, reporting the one thing indistinguishable from a substituted payload, so the investigation is of an attack that never happened. Round-trip tests in either language alone pass forever because each agrees with itself. Exclude the characters at the shared schema rather than stripping them before signing, and pin the exact canonical byte string as a literal in BOTH test suites. HIGH.
- [A working shutdown handler looks broken, because process.exit() discards the line that proves it](process-exit-truncates-shutdown-log.md): stdout is ASYNC on a pipe, so process.exit() throws away the buffered "drain complete" line while the earlier "SIGTERM received" survives -- every visible signal says the drain was cut off when it may have finished perfectly. Compounded by wrappers rewriting the exit code (sh -> 143, doppler run -> 255), so the code proves nothing either, and by `sh -c "a || b"` being unable to exec, which leaves the SHELL as the supervised process. Also: `kill -TERM <pid>` tests forwarding down a chain, while dumb-init broadcasts to the process GROUP -- a layer can pass the first and fail the second, so the local proof is of the wrong question. Use process.exitCode + closeIdleConnections(), exec the app, and trust an app-level log line over the exit code. HIGH.
- [Attaching shared WebSocket wiring to two HTTP listeners double-registers every process-wide subscriber](attach-per-listener-double-registers.md): `attachWebSocketServers(httpServer)` reads as per-listener setup, but constructing the WSS instances, subscribing to the cluster bus and starting the heartbeat sweeps are per-PROCESS -- so calling it for a plaintext listener and again for an mTLS one registers the bus subscriber twice against the same module-level socket map, and every message relayed to a peer is written to its one socket twice. Nothing errors and each duplicate is individually valid, so it is invisible in metrics and reads as a bug in the receiver. Seen live: every desktop-agent command executed twice, and two `remote_session_start_host` pushes raced two host processes for one session -- the loser spent the single-use credential, was refused close 4401, and killed the session. The tell is one-time boot lines printed twice in a single process's startup log. Split once-per-process from once-per-listener, memoize the PROMISE (clearing it on rejection), and assert both halves: registered once, still upgrading on every listener. HIGH.
- [npx does not forward SIGTERM, so the container's graceful shutdown never runs](npx-does-not-forward-sigterm.md): `npx <tool> app.js` as a container CMD looks equivalent to running the binary, but npx never delivers SIGTERM to the process it spawns, so the drain handler never fires -- connections stay open and spawned children are orphaned on every deploy. All three things you would check read as normal: no shutdown logs (indistinguishable from a platform that stops collecting stdout at teardown), a SIGTERM-to-gone time exactly equal to the configured grace period (looks like a drain window being used, not a timeout being hit -- its CONSTANCY is the tell), and exit 143, which plenty of healthy containers exit with. A forwarding wrapper (`doppler run --forward-signals`, `tini -g`, a trapping shell) masks it entirely, so deleting that wrapper for an unrelated reason is what exposes it. dumb-init does not help: it delivers to npx and npx is where the signal stops, with or without --single-child. Verify in a container, never with `kill -TERM <npx-pid>` on the host -- that path reports FORWARDED and is the wrong question. Call the binary directly (absolute path: npm workspaces hoists to the repo-root node_modules). HIGH.
